content: The text provided appears to be a long list of references and technical details related to studies, guidelines, and reports on micronutrient interventions, anemia, and public health nutrition. 1. A study conducted in Kenya demonstrated that a micronutrient powder containing low-dose iron in the form of NaFeEDTA, but excluding amaranth grain flour, effectively reduced anemia and iron deficiency among preschool children. (J Nutr. 2012;142(9):1756–63). 2. Simulation models in Kenya evaluated the impact of maize porridge fortified with either grain amaranth or a micronutrient powder containing NaFeEDTA on iron intake and status in children. The findings highlighted the potential benefits of such fortification strategies. (Public Health Nutr. 2013;16(9):1605–13). 3. In rural Haiti, the feasibility of delivering micronutrient Sprinkles through a food-assisted maternal and child health and nutrition program was assessed using program theory. This approach provided insights into the practical implementation of such interventions. (Matern Child Nutr. 2009;5(1):33–48). 4. A study in rural Haiti demonstrated that micronutrient Sprinkles, when integrated into a health and nutrition program, significantly reduced anemia among children aged 9 to 24 months. (J Nutr. 2007;137(4):1023–30). 5. Research in North India examined compliance with home-based fortification strategies for delivering iron and zinc. The study revealed improvements in hematological and growth markers among children aged 6 to 24 months. (J Health Popul Nutr. 2014;32(2):217–26). 6. The Pakistan Sprinkles Diarrhoea Study found that micronutrient powders, including zinc, reduced the incidence of diarrhea in children. (Arch Dis Child. 2006;91(7):573–9). 7. A cluster-randomized trial in Pakistan evaluated the effects of daily supplementation with zinc, iron, and other micronutrients on growth and morbidity in young children. The intervention showed significant benefits. (Lancet. 2013;382(9886):29–40). 8. A study in Honduras assessed the acceptance and impact of ferrous fumarate-containing micronutrient Sprinkles on anemia, iron deficiency, and anthropometric outcomes in children. The results indicated positive effects on nutritional status. (In: Silverberg D, editor. Anemia). 9. A preschool-based pilot trial in South Africa highlighted lessons learned from implementing point-of-use micronutrient fortification. The intervention demonstrated improvements in nutritional outcomes. (Int J Food Sci Nutr. 2011;62(1):1–16). 10. The World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines on the use of multiple micronutrient powders for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by infants and young children aged 6–23 months and children aged 2–12 years. These guidelines aim to address anemia and micronutrient deficiencies. (WHO guideline). 11. A study in rural Himalayan villages of India evaluated the acceptability of micronutrient-fortified school meals among schoolchildren. The intervention improved vitamin A, folate, and iron status. (J Nutr. 2010;140(6):1146–54). 12. Research in China demonstrated that short-term daily or weekly administration of micronutrient Sprinkles achieved high compliance and did not result in iron overload among schoolchildren. (Public Health Nutr. 2006;9(3):336–44). 13. A micronutrient powder containing low doses of highly absorbable iron and zinc was shown to reduce deficiencies and improve weight-for-age Z-scores in South African children. (J Nutr. 2011;141(2):237–42). 14. A controlled trial in India evaluated the community-level fortification of a food supplement with multiple micronutrients among preschool children aged 36–66 months. The intervention improved nutritional status. (Am J Clin Nutr. 2007;85(4):1127–33). 15. The efficacy of fortifying school meals with ferrous glycine phosphate and riboflavin was assessed in India. The intervention reduced anemia and angular stomatitis among schoolchildren. (Food Nutr Bull. 2009;30(3):260–4). 16. WHO and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) published guidelines on vitamin and mineral requirements in human nutrition, emphasizing the importance of addressing deficiencies in vulnerable populations. (WHO/FAO publication). 17. The WHO's guideline on daily iron supplementation in infants and children provides evidence-based recommendations to prevent and treat iron deficiency anemia. (WHO guideline). 18. The Integrated Global Action Plan for Pneumonia and Diarrhoea (GAPPD) outlines strategies to end preventable child deaths from these conditions by 2025. (WHO publication). 19. The WHO's Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System (VMNIS) serves as a resource for monitoring and addressing micronutrient deficiencies globally. (WHO VMNIS). 20. The WHO's handbook for guideline development provides a framework for creating evidence-based recommendations in public health. (WHO handbook). 21. The AGREE II instrument advances the development, reporting, and evaluation of healthcare guidelines, ensuring their quality and applicability. (CMAJ. 2010;182(18):E839–42). 22. The WHO's manual on micronutrient powder composition offers guidelines for defining the nutrient content of single-serve sachets for populations with high anemia prevalence. (WHO manual). 23. A practical guide on implementation research in health provides tools for developing and scaling up effective public health interventions. (WHO publication). 24. The WHO's logic model for micronutrient interventions in public health outlines a systematic approach to planning, implementing, and evaluating such programs. (WHO logic model).
